points: Lexical analysis breaks the source into tokens such as keywords, identifiers, operators and literals.
Whitespace and comments are removed, and a symbol table of identifiers is begun.
Syntax analysis checks that the sequence of tokens conforms to the grammar of the language.
A parse tree or abstract syntax tree is constructed, and any violation is reported as a syntax error.

practice.q: State the difference between a syntax error and a semantic error, giving an example of each.
points: A syntax error breaks the grammatical rules of the language, for example a missing closing bracket.
A semantic error is grammatically valid but meaningless, for example adding a number to a string, or using an undeclared variable.
Syntax errors are found during syntax analysis; semantic errors are found during semantic analysis.

practice.q: Explain why languages such as Java and Python compile to bytecode rather than directly to machine code.
points: Machine code is specific to one processor family, so a directly compiled program is not portable.
Bytecode is compiled once and can run on any machine with a suitable virtual machine.
Much of the analysis and optimisation is done at compile time, so it is faster than interpreting source directly.
The virtual machine can also compile hot bytecode to machine code at run time, recovering much of the remaining speed.

practice.q: A company is choosing between a compiled and an interpreted language for software to be sold to customers. Discuss the factors they should weigh.
points: A compiled program runs faster, which matters if performance is a selling point.
Distributing an executable does not reveal the source code, protecting intellectual property.
However a separate executable must be built for each target platform, increasing maintenance.
An interpreted language runs anywhere the interpreter exists, and shortens development time.
A reasoned judgement is reached, weighing performance and secrecy against portability and development cost.

pages.title: What a computer actually is
pages.lede: Before any of the detail, the one idea the whole subject rests on — a machine that stores its own instructions and follows them without understanding them.

cards.q: What is a stored-program computer?
cards.a: A machine that holds both its **data and its instructions** in the same memory, and works through those instructions one at a time. Changing what it does means changing the contents of memory, not the wiring.

cards.q: Why does it matter that instructions live in the same memory as data?
cards.a: Because a program becomes something the machine can *store, copy and change* like any other data. It is what makes a computer general-purpose rather than a fixed appliance.

cards.q: What are the four things every computer does?
cards.a: **Input**, **processing**, **storage**, **output**. Everything else in the course is detail hanging off one of those four.

cards.q: Does a computer understand the instructions it follows?
cards.a: No. Each instruction is a pattern of bits that causes a fixed electrical effect. Meaning exists only in the mind of the programmer.

cards.q: What is the difference between hardware and software?
cards.a: Hardware is the physical machinery; software is the pattern of bits in memory that tells it what to do. The same hardware runs any software you load into it.

cards.q: What is a bit?
cards.a: One of two distinguishable states, written $0$ and $1$. Physically it is a voltage that is either low or high — never anything in between, by design.

cards.q: Why do computers use two states rather than ten?
cards.a: Because telling *low* from *high* survives noise, heat and manufacturing variation. Distinguishing ten voltage levels reliably, billions of times a second, does not.

cards.q: What does "general-purpose" mean?
cards.a: One machine that can be made to do any computable task by loading a different program, rather than being built for one job.

cards.q: In one sentence, what is an algorithm?
cards.a: A finite sequence of unambiguous steps that turns an input into the intended output.

cards.q: Why is a pocket calculator not a general-purpose computer?
cards.a: Its behaviour is fixed by its wiring. You cannot load a new program into it and make it do something its designers did not build in.

practice.q: State what is meant by a **stored-program computer**.
points: Instructions are held in memory alongside the data / in the same memory as data.
The processor fetches and executes those instructions one at a time / in sequence.

practice.q: Explain why storing instructions in memory makes a computer general-purpose.
points: A program is just data in memory, so it can be loaded, replaced or changed.
Changing the task therefore requires no change to the hardware / no rewiring.
One machine can therefore perform any task for which a program can be written.

practice.q: A student says "the computer understands my Python program". Explain why this is not accurate, referring to what the processor actually does.
points: The processor only ever acts on patterns of bits / binary instructions.
Each instruction causes a fixed electrical effect in the hardware, with no meaning attached.
Python must first be translated into those instructions before anything can run.
Meaning is supplied by the programmer, not the machine / the machine has no model of the problem.

practice.q: Identify the four stages of the general computing model and give an example of each in a supermarket self-checkout.
points: Input — scanning a barcode / touching the screen / inserting a card.
Processing — looking up the price, adding to the total, checking the payment.
Output — the display, the receipt, the printed label (storage also credited if described).

practice.q: Explain why digital computers represent information using two states rather than ten.
points: Two states can be represented by a voltage being clearly low or clearly high.
This tolerates noise, temperature change and manufacturing variation, because a small drift does not change which state is read.
Ten levels would need the circuit to distinguish much smaller differences reliably.
Errors would therefore be far more frequent at the speeds and scales involved.

practice.q: Distinguish between hardware and software, and explain why the distinction is less sharp than it first appears.
points: Hardware is the physical machinery; software is the instructions and data held in memory.
The same hardware performs completely different tasks depending on the software loaded.
The boundary blurs — firmware, and hardware that is itself configurable — so the distinction is about role rather than substance.

practice.q: A washing machine contains a processor, memory and a program. Discuss whether it should be called a computer.
points: It does contain the components of a computer — processor, memory, stored instructions.
It performs input, processing and output, so it fits the general model.
However its program is fixed and cannot be replaced by the user, so it is an embedded system.
It is therefore a computer in construction but special-purpose in use.
A defensible conclusion is stated either way, supported by the points above.

pages.title: Inside the processor
pages.lede: The four parts every CPU has, what each one is physically for, and why the design has barely changed in eighty years.

cards.q: What are the main components of a CPU?
cards.a: The **control unit**, the **arithmetic and logic unit**, a set of **registers**, and the **buses** connecting them to memory.

cards.q: What does the control unit do?
cards.a: It decodes each instruction and sends the timing and control signals that make the rest of the hardware carry it out. It computes nothing itself — it is the conductor, not a player.

cards.q: What does the ALU do?
cards.a: Arithmetic ($+$, $-$, and often $\times$) and logic (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons, shifts). It is where the actual work happens.

cards.q: What is a register?
cards.a: A very small, very fast store inside the CPU itself — typically 32 or 64 bits. Reaching one costs a fraction of a nanosecond, against tens of nanoseconds for main memory.

cards.q: What does the program counter (PC) hold?
cards.a: The **address of the next instruction** to fetch. Not the instruction — the address of it.

cards.q: What does the memory address register (MAR) hold?
cards.a: The address currently being read from or written to. It is what drives the address bus.

cards.q: What does the memory data register (MDR) hold?
cards.a: The data just read from memory, or about to be written to it. Everything travelling between the CPU and memory passes through it.

cards.q: What does the accumulator hold?
cards.a: The result of the ALU's most recent operation, ready to be used by the next one or written back to memory.

cards.q: What is the current instruction register (CIR)?
cards.a: The register holding the instruction currently being decoded and executed.

cards.q: What are the three buses and what does each carry?
cards.a: **Address bus** — which location (one way, CPU to memory). **Data bus** — the value itself (two way). **Control bus** — signals such as read, write and clock (mixed).

cards.q: Why is the address bus one-directional but the data bus two-directional?
cards.a: Only the CPU ever says which address it wants, so addresses travel one way. Data travels out on a write and in on a read, so it needs both.

cards.q: How does the width of the address bus limit a computer?
cards.a: $n$ address lines can name $2^n$ locations. A 32-bit address bus can therefore reach only $2^{32}$ bytes, which is 4 GiB — the historical reason for the move to 64-bit.

practice.q: Describe the role of the control unit and the arithmetic and logic unit, making clear how they differ.
points: The control unit decodes instructions and issues control signals to the other components.
It sequences and coordinates operations, including timing, but performs no calculation itself.
The ALU performs arithmetic operations such as addition and subtraction.
The ALU also performs logical operations and comparisons, producing the results and status flags.

practice.q: Explain why registers are used at all, given that the computer already has main memory.
points: Registers are inside the CPU, so access takes a fraction of the time main memory does.
Instructions need somewhere to hold operands and intermediate results while executing.
Using main memory for this would leave the CPU waiting on every step, wasting most of its speed.

practice.q: State the purpose of the program counter, the memory address register, the memory data register and the current instruction register.
points: PC — holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
MAR — holds the address of the memory location currently being accessed.
MDR — holds the data being transferred to or from memory.
CIR — holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.

practice.q: A processor has a 16-bit address bus and an 8-bit data bus. Calculate the maximum memory it can address, and state the units.
points: $2^{16} = 65{,}536$ addressable locations.
Each location holds 8 bits, that is one byte, because the data bus is 8 bits wide.
Maximum addressable memory is therefore $65{,}536$ bytes, that is 64 KiB.

practice.q: Explain why the address bus is unidirectional while the data bus is bidirectional.
points: The CPU is always the component that specifies which address is wanted.
Memory never sends an address back, so a return path would be unused.
Data must travel from memory to the CPU when reading.
Data must travel from the CPU to memory when writing, so both directions are needed.

practice.q: Explain what the control bus is for, giving two examples of signals it carries.
points: It carries the signals that coordinate and time the actions of the components.
Example — a read or write signal telling memory which operation is wanted.
Example — the clock signal, or an interrupt request, which synchronises or redirects activity.

practice.q: A manufacturer widens a processor's data bus from 32 bits to 64 bits, leaving the clock speed unchanged. Discuss the effect on performance.
points: Twice as much data moves between CPU and memory per transfer.
Programs handling large values or large blocks of data need fewer transfers, so they run faster.
Programs limited by something else — dependent calculations, or waiting on input — see little or no gain.
The wider bus costs more in pins, tracks and power, so the benefit is not free.
A supported conclusion is reached, for example that the benefit depends on whether the workload is memory-bound.

pages.title: The fetch–decode–execute cycle
pages.lede: The loop the processor has been running since you turned the machine on, traced register by register until there is nothing mysterious left in it.

cards.q: What are the three stages of the machine cycle?
cards.a: **Fetch** the next instruction from memory, **decode** it to work out what it means, **execute** it. Then repeat, forever.

cards.q: Write out the fetch stage as register transfers.
cards.a: $\text{MAR} \leftarrow \text{PC}$; then memory is read so $\text{MDR} \leftarrow [\text{MAR}]$; then $\text{CIR} \leftarrow \text{MDR}$; and $\text{PC} \leftarrow \text{PC} + 1$.

cards.q: When is the program counter incremented, and why then?
cards.a: During the **fetch** stage, right after the address has been used. Doing it early means a jump instruction executed later can simply overwrite the PC, without the increment undoing it.

cards.q: What happens during decode?
cards.a: The control unit splits the instruction in the CIR into its **opcode** (what to do) and its **operand** (what to do it to), and works out which control signals the operation needs.

cards.q: What is an opcode?
cards.a: The part of an instruction saying which operation is wanted — load, store, add, jump. Typically the first few bits.

cards.q: What is an operand?
cards.a: The part of an instruction saying what to operate on: a value, a register, or more often the address of one.

cards.q: How does a jump instruction work, mechanically?
cards.a: Execute writes the jump's operand into the **program counter**. The next fetch therefore starts somewhere else. That is the whole mechanism behind every loop, `if` and function call.

cards.q: What is the clock speed of a processor?
cards.a: How many cycles it performs per second, measured in hertz. $3\,\text{GHz}$ is $3\times10^{9}$ cycles a second.

cards.q: Does one clock cycle equal one instruction?
cards.a: No. Simple designs take several cycles per instruction; pipelined ones complete more than one per cycle on a good run. Clock speed alone does not tell you how fast a processor is.

cards.q: What is pipelining?
cards.a: Overlapping the stages, so one instruction is being executed while the next is decoded and a third is fetched — like a production line rather than one worker doing every step.

cards.q: Why can a branch hurt a pipeline?
cards.a: The instructions already fetched behind a jump turn out to be the wrong ones and must be discarded, leaving the pipeline to refill.

practice.q: Describe the fetch stage of the machine cycle, referring to the registers involved.
points: The address in the program counter is copied into the memory address register.
The instruction at that address is read from memory into the memory data register.
The instruction is copied from the MDR into the current instruction register.
The program counter is incremented so it points at the following instruction.

practice.q: Explain why the program counter is incremented during fetch rather than at the end of the cycle.
points: The address it held has already been used, so it is free to update.
If the instruction turns out to be a jump, execute can overwrite the PC and the increment will not interfere with it.

practice.q: Explain what happens during the decode stage.
points: The instruction held in the CIR is split into opcode and operand.
The control unit interprets the opcode to determine which operation is required.
It then generates the control signals needed by the ALU, registers and memory for that operation.

practice.q: A program contains a loop. Explain, in terms of the machine cycle, how the processor repeats instructions.
points: At the end of the loop body there is a jump or branch instruction.
During its execute stage, the operand is written into the program counter.
The next fetch therefore takes its address from the start of the loop rather than the following line.
The cycle continues as normal from there, so the same instructions are fetched again.

practice.q: Two processors are advertised at 2.5 GHz and 3.5 GHz. Explain why the second is not necessarily 40% faster.
points: Clock speed only counts cycles, not work completed per cycle.
Processors differ in how many cycles each instruction takes, and in how effectively they pipeline.
Cache size and memory speed may leave either processor waiting, whatever its clock.
The number of cores, and whether the software can use them, may matter more than clock speed.

practice.q: Explain what pipelining is and why a conditional branch reduces its benefit.
points: Pipelining overlaps the stages of consecutive instructions rather than completing one before starting the next.
While one instruction executes, the next is decoded and a third is fetched.
Throughput therefore rises, approaching one completed instruction per cycle.
At a conditional branch the processor does not yet know which instructions follow, so it may fetch the wrong ones.
Those partially processed instructions must be discarded and the pipeline refilled, costing the cycles that had been saved.

practice.q: State what is held in the MAR, the MDR and the CIR immediately after the fetch stage of an instruction stored at address 40.
points: MAR holds 40, the address that was just accessed.
MDR holds the instruction that was read from address 40.
CIR holds that same instruction, copied there ready for decoding.

pages.title: Primary memory and the hierarchy
pages.lede: Why a computer has five kinds of memory instead of one good one, and why the answer is economics rather than engineering.

cards.q: What is primary memory?
cards.a: Memory the processor can address directly — RAM and ROM. Anything the CPU works on must be here first.

cards.q: What does volatile mean?
cards.a: The contents are lost when power is removed. RAM is volatile; ROM and secondary storage are not.

cards.q: What is RAM used for?
cards.a: Holding the programs currently running and the data they are working on. It is read/write and volatile.

cards.q: What is ROM used for?
cards.a: Holding the instructions needed to start the machine — the bootstrap or firmware. Non-volatile, so something is there before anything has been loaded.

cards.q: Why does a computer need ROM as well as RAM?
cards.a: At power-on RAM is empty and there is no operating system yet. Something non-volatile must hold the first instructions, or the machine could never start.

cards.q: What is cache memory?
cards.a: A small amount of very fast SRAM between the CPU and main memory, holding recently and frequently used data so the CPU waits less often.

cards.q: Put registers, cache, RAM and secondary storage in order of speed.
cards.a: Registers (fastest, smallest, dearest), then cache, then RAM, then secondary storage (slowest, largest, cheapest). Speed, cost per bit and capacity all trade against each other.

cards.q: What is a cache hit and a cache miss?
cards.a: A **hit** is finding the wanted data already in cache. A **miss** means fetching it from slower memory — and the delay of a miss is why hit rate matters so much.

cards.q: What is locality of reference?
cards.a: The observation that programs tend to reuse the same data soon (**temporal**) and to use data stored nearby (**spatial**). Caching only works because this is true.

cards.q: What is virtual memory?
cards.a: Using part of secondary storage as though it were extra RAM, so programs larger than physical memory can run. Far slower, because the disc is involved.

cards.q: What is disc thrashing?
cards.a: When there is so little real RAM that the machine spends most of its time swapping pages in and out of virtual memory rather than doing useful work.

cards.q: Why not build a computer entirely from registers?
cards.a: Cost and physics. Register-speed storage needs about six transistors per bit and must sit close to the CPU; a machine with gigabytes of it would be unaffordable and too large to stay fast.

practice.q: Compare RAM and ROM, referring to volatility, whether they can be written to, and their typical use.
points: RAM is volatile, losing its contents when power is removed; ROM is non-volatile and retains them.
RAM can be read and written freely during normal operation.
ROM cannot be written to in normal use, or only through a special procedure.
RAM holds running programs and their data; ROM holds start-up instructions or firmware.

practice.q: Explain why a computer cannot start up with RAM alone.
points: RAM is volatile, so at power-on it contains nothing usable.
The processor must have instructions to fetch immediately, before any software has been loaded.
Those first instructions must therefore be held in non-volatile memory such as ROM.

practice.q: Explain how cache memory improves performance, using the terms hit, miss and locality of reference.
points: Cache holds copies of recently or frequently accessed data and instructions.
A hit means the CPU finds what it needs in cache and avoids the much slower main memory access.
Programs display locality of reference, reusing the same data and data stored nearby, so hits are common.
A miss costs the full main-memory access, so overall benefit depends on the hit rate being high.

practice.q: A computer has a cache with a hit rate of 90%. A cache access takes 2 ns and a main memory access takes 60 ns. Calculate the average access time and comment on the result.
points: Average $= 0.9 \times 2 + 0.1 \times 60$.
This is far closer to cache speed than to memory speed, despite one access in ten missing.
The remaining 10% of accesses contribute most of the time, so raising the hit rate further has a large effect.

practice.q: Explain why the memory in a computer is arranged as a hierarchy rather than as a single type.
points: Fast memory is expensive per bit and cannot be provided in large quantities affordably.
Large cheap memory is slow, and using it alone would leave the processor waiting.
A hierarchy gives a small amount of fast memory in front of a large amount of slow memory, approaching the speed of the first at close to the cost of the second.

practice.q: Explain what virtual memory is and describe one drawback of relying on it.
points: Part of secondary storage is used as though it were additional RAM.
Pages of data are moved between RAM and the disc as they are needed, so programs larger than physical memory can run.
Secondary storage is orders of magnitude slower than RAM, so performance drops when it is used heavily.
In the extreme the system thrashes, spending most of its time swapping rather than doing useful work.

practice.q: A laptop with 8 GB of RAM becomes very slow when several large applications are open. Explain what is happening and evaluate two possible responses.
points: The combined demand exceeds physical RAM, so the operating system moves pages to virtual memory on the disc.
Access to swapped pages is far slower than RAM, and in the worst case the machine thrashes.
Installing more RAM addresses the cause directly and lets more of the working set stay in memory.
Closing applications reduces demand immediately and costs nothing, but limits what the user can do at once.
A reasoned judgement is given, for example that more RAM is the better long-term fix if the workload is genuinely needed.

pages.title: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
pages.lede: Counting in a base other than ten, why machines count in two, and why programmers write in sixteen.

cards.q: What is the base of a number system?
cards.a: How many distinct digits it uses, and therefore the multiplier between one column and the next. Base 10 uses $0$–$9$; base 2 uses $0$–$1$; base 16 uses $0$–$F$.

cards.q: What is the place value of each column in binary?
cards.a: Powers of two, rising right to left: $1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128$.

cards.q: Convert $1011\,0110_2$ to denary.
How do you convert denary to binary?
cards.a: Repeatedly divide by 2 and record the remainders, then read them **bottom to top**. Or subtract the largest power of two that fits, and repeat.

cards.q: Why is hexadecimal used?
cards.a: One hex digit is exactly four bits, so a byte is exactly two hex digits. It is far shorter than binary to write and far less error-prone to read, with no loss of information.

cards.q: What are the hex digits above 9?
Convert $\text{2F}_{16}$ to denary.
How do you convert binary to hex quickly?
cards.a: Split into groups of four bits from the right, then write each group as one hex digit. $1011\,0110_2 = \text{B6}_{16}$.

cards.q: What is a nibble?
cards.a: Four bits — half a byte, and exactly one hexadecimal digit.

cards.q: How many values can $n$ bits represent?
cards.a: $2^n$. Eight bits give $2^8 = 256$ values, that is $0$ to $255$.

cards.q: What is the difference between a kilobyte and a kibibyte?
cards.a: $1\,\text{kB} = 1000$ bytes; $1\,\text{KiB} = 1024$ bytes. Memory is counted in powers of two, storage is usually sold in powers of ten.

practice.q: Convert the binary number $1101\,0011_2$ to denary, showing your working.
points: Place values identified as $128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1$.
Correct answer $211$.

practice.q: Convert the denary number $173$ to binary, showing your method.
points: A valid method is shown, either repeated division by 2 or subtraction of descending powers of two.
Working is correct at each step.
Correct answer $1010\,1101_2$.

practice.q: Convert $\text{9C}_{16}$ to denary.
points: $9 \times 16 = 144$ and $\text{C} = 12$.
Correct answer $156$.

practice.q: Explain why hexadecimal is used by programmers in preference to binary, when the machine itself uses neither.
points: One hex digit corresponds exactly to four bits, so conversion is direct and needs no arithmetic.
Hex is about a quarter the length of the equivalent binary, so it is quicker to write and easier to read without losing a digit.
No information is lost or approximated, unlike denary, where the correspondence to bits is not direct.

practice.q: A colour is stored as three bytes, one each for red, green and blue. Calculate how many distinct colours can be represented, and express the colour $\text{FF}\,\text{8C}\,00_{16}$ as three denary values.
points: Each byte gives $2^8 = 256$ levels.
$\text{FF} = 255$ and $\text{8C} = 140$.
So red $255$, green $140$, blue $0$.

practice.q: A file is described as 2 MB by its creator but shows as 1.91 MB in a file manager. Explain why.
points: One uses powers of ten, where $1\,\text{MB} = 1{,}000{,}000$ bytes.
The other uses powers of two, where the unit is $1{,}048{,}576$ bytes.
$2{,}000{,}000 \div 1{,}048{,}576 \approx 1.91$, so both figures describe the same file.

practice.q: A system uses 12 bits to store an unsigned integer. State the range of values it can hold, and explain what happens if the program tries to store 5000.
points: $2^{12} = 4096$ possible values.
Range is $0$ to $4095$ inclusive.
$5000$ exceeds the maximum, so it cannot be represented in 12 bits.
The value overflows and the stored result is wrong, typically wrapping round rather than raising an error.

pages.title: Negative numbers and two's complement
pages.lede: How to write a minus sign using only zeros and ones, and why the obvious method was abandoned for a stranger one that makes subtraction free.

cards.q: What is sign and magnitude?
cards.a: Use the leftmost bit as a sign ($0$ positive, $1$ negative) and the rest as the size. Simple to read, but it gives two zeros and needs separate circuitry for subtraction.

cards.q: Why was sign and magnitude abandoned?
cards.a: It has $+0$ and $-0$, wasting a pattern and complicating comparisons, and adding a positive to a negative needs a special subtractor rather than the ordinary adder.

cards.q: How do you form the two's complement of a binary number?
cards.a: **Invert every bit, then add one.** Equivalently, copy bits from the right up to and including the first $1$, then invert everything to the left of it.

cards.q: What is $-40$ in 8-bit two's complement?
What is the range of an $n$-bit two's complement number?
cards.a: $-2^{n-1}$ to $+2^{n-1}-1$. For eight bits that is $-128$ to $+127$.

cards.q: Why is the negative range one larger than the positive?
cards.a: There is only one zero, so the $2^n$ patterns split into zero, $2^{n-1}-1$ positives and $2^{n-1}$ negatives.

cards.q: How do you read a negative two's complement number back to denary?
cards.a: Either apply invert-and-add-one again and negate the result, or treat the leading column as negative: in eight bits it is worth $-128$ rather than $+128$.

cards.q: Why does two's complement make subtraction free?
cards.a: Because $a - b$ is just $a + (-b)$, and negation is invert-and-add-one. One adder circuit handles both operations, so no subtractor is needed.

cards.q: How do you detect overflow in two's complement addition?
cards.a: When two numbers of the **same** sign produce a result of the **opposite** sign. Adding a positive to a negative can never overflow.

cards.q: What is an arithmetic shift left, and what does it do to the value?
cards.a: Shift every bit left one place and put a $0$ in at the right. It multiplies by two, provided the value does not overflow.

cards.q: What is an arithmetic shift right?
cards.a: Shift right and copy the **sign bit** into the vacated position, so negatives stay negative. It divides by two, rounding towards negative infinity.

practice.q: Convert $-53$ to 8-bit two's complement, showing your working.
points: Adding one gives $1100\,1011_2$.

practice.q: The 8-bit two's complement value $1001\,0110_2$ is stored. State its denary value.
points: Recognises the leading $1$ as negative and applies a correct method.
Correct answer $-106$.

practice.q: State the range of values that can be stored in a 16-bit two's complement integer, and explain how the range is derived.
points: There are $2^{16} = 65{,}536$ patterns available.
Half represent negatives and half zero-or-positive, giving $-2^{15}$ to $+2^{15}-1$.

practice.q: Explain why two's complement is used in preference to sign and magnitude.
points: Sign and magnitude produces two representations of zero, wasting a pattern and complicating equality tests.
Two's complement has a single zero.
In two's complement, subtraction can be performed by negating and adding.
One adder circuit therefore performs both addition and subtraction, reducing hardware cost and complexity.

practice.q: Add $0110\,1001_2$ and $0101\,0011_2$ as 8-bit two's complement values. State the result and explain whether overflow has occurred.
points: Correct binary addition giving $1011\,1100_2$.
Both operands are positive, since both begin with $0$.
The result begins with $1$, so it is negative.
Two positives producing a negative means overflow has occurred and the result is invalid.

practice.q: Explain why an arithmetic shift right copies the sign bit rather than inserting a zero.
points: Inserting a zero would clear the sign bit and turn a negative number positive.
Copying the sign bit preserves the sign of the value.
This keeps the operation equivalent to division by two for negative numbers as well as positive ones.

practice.q: A temperature sensor stores readings as 8-bit two's complement values in tenths of a degree. Explain the consequences of this choice and suggest an improvement.
points: The representable range is $-128$ to $+127$ in tenths, that is $-12.8$ to $+12.7$ degrees.
Any temperature outside that range cannot be stored and would overflow.
Overflow wraps silently, so a high temperature could be recorded as a low or negative one.
Using 16 bits would extend the range to roughly $\pm 3276$ degrees, comfortably sufficient.
Alternatively, store whole degrees, or add range checking before storing, though each has its own cost in precision or complexity.

pages.title: Representing text
pages.lede: How letters became numbers, why that nearly broke the internet for most of the world, and how Unicode fixed it.

cards.q: How is text stored in a computer?
cards.a: Each character is assigned a number by a **character set**, and that number is stored in binary. There is nothing letter-like in the bits at all.

cards.q: What is ASCII?
cards.a: A 7-bit character set defining 128 characters — English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes. Usually stored in one byte with the top bit spare.

cards.q: How many characters can ASCII represent, and why is that a problem?
cards.a: $2^7 = 128$. It covers English and almost nothing else — no accents, no Greek, no Arabic, no Chinese.

cards.q: What is the ASCII code for "A" and for "a"?
cards.a: $65$ for `A` and $97$ for `a`. They differ by $32$, which is a single bit, so changing case is one bitwise operation.

cards.q: Why are the digits $0$–$9$ at codes $48$–$57$?
cards.a: So that the character code minus $48$ gives the numeric value. The low four bits of the code are the digit in binary.

cards.q: What is Unicode?
cards.a: A character set assigning a unique **code point** to every character in every writing system — over 150,000 of them, with room for more than a million.

cards.q: What is the difference between a character set and an encoding?
cards.a: The **character set** says which number belongs to which character. The **encoding** says how that number is written as bytes. Unicode is the set; UTF-8 and UTF-16 are encodings of it.

cards.q: What is UTF-8 and why is it dominant?
cards.a: A variable-length encoding using one to four bytes per character. ASCII characters take exactly one byte and are unchanged, so existing English text is already valid UTF-8.

cards.q: What is the disadvantage of Unicode compared with ASCII?
cards.a: Text can take more space — up to four bytes a character — and characters are no longer a fixed width, so you cannot find the $n$th character by jumping to byte $n$.

cards.q: Why does the same text file sometimes appear as gibberish?
cards.a: It is being read with a different encoding from the one it was written in, so the bytes are grouped and interpreted wrongly.

practice.q: Explain how the word "Cat" is stored in a computer using ASCII.
points: Each character is looked up in the character set to give a numeric code.
Each code is stored in binary in one byte, so three bytes are used in total.

practice.q: State the number of distinct characters that can be represented in 7 bits and in 8 bits.
points: 7 bits gives $2^7 = 128$ characters.
8 bits gives $2^8 = 256$ characters.

practice.q: Explain why ASCII was insufficient for worldwide use, and how Unicode addresses the problem.
points: ASCII has only 128 codes, enough for English but not for accented, non-Latin or logographic scripts.
Different regions produced incompatible extensions, so the same byte meant different characters in different places.
Unicode assigns a unique code point to every character across all writing systems.
A document can therefore mix scripts and be read identically anywhere, with no ambiguity about which set is in use.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a character set and a character encoding, using Unicode and UTF-8 as your example.
points: A character set maps characters to numbers, called code points.
An encoding specifies how those numbers are represented as a sequence of bytes.
Unicode is the character set; UTF-8 is one way of encoding its code points into bytes.

practice.q: Explain two advantages of UTF-8 over a fixed 4-byte encoding of Unicode.
points: UTF-8 uses one byte for ASCII characters, so English text is a quarter of the size.
Existing ASCII files are already valid UTF-8, so old data and software continue to work.
Less storage and bandwidth are needed for the majority of web content.
A fixed 4-byte encoding wastes three bytes in four for plain English, with no benefit to most users.

practice.q: A program converts a lowercase letter to uppercase by subtracting 32 from its ASCII code. Explain why this works and state one situation in which it fails.
points: Uppercase and lowercase letters are 32 apart in ASCII, so subtracting 32 moves from one to the other.
$32$ is $2^5$, so the operation only clears a single bit.
It fails for any character that is not a lowercase letter, such as a digit or an accented character, where it produces a different character entirely.

practice.q: A messaging app stores messages in UTF-8 and limits them to 280 bytes. Discuss the effect on users writing in different languages.
points: English characters take one byte, so a user can send close to 280 characters.
Accented and Greek or Cyrillic characters take two bytes, halving the effective limit.
Chinese, Japanese and emoji take three or four bytes, reducing it to around 70–90 characters.
The limit is therefore unfair between languages, and counting characters rather than bytes would be more equitable.

pages.title: Images and sound
pages.lede: Turning something continuous — a scene, a pressure wave — into a finite list of numbers, and what is unavoidably lost in the process.

cards.q: What is a pixel?
cards.a: The smallest addressable element of a bitmap image. The whole image is a grid of them, each storing one colour.

cards.q: What is image resolution?
cards.a: The number of pixels in the image, usually given as width $\times$ height. More pixels means more detail and a proportionally larger file.

cards.q: What is colour depth?
cards.a: The number of bits used per pixel. $n$ bits give $2^n$ possible colours; 24-bit colour gives $2^{24} \approx 16.7$ million.

cards.q: Give the formula for the size of an uncompressed bitmap.
cards.a: $\text{size} = \text{width} \times \text{height} \times \text{colour depth}$, in bits. Divide by $8$ for bytes.

cards.q: What is metadata in an image file?
cards.a: Data about the image rather than the image itself — dimensions, colour depth, date, camera settings. The file needs it to be interpretable at all.

cards.q: What is sampling, in the context of sound?
cards.a: Measuring the amplitude of the sound wave at regular intervals and storing each measurement as a number.

cards.q: What is sample rate?
cards.a: How many samples are taken per second, in hertz. CD audio uses $44{,}100\,\text{Hz}$.

cards.q: What is bit depth in audio?
cards.a: How many bits store each sample. More bits give finer amplitude steps and a lower quantisation error.

cards.q: Give the formula for the size of an uncompressed audio file.
cards.a: $\text{size} = \text{sample rate} \times \text{bit depth} \times \text{channels} \times \text{seconds}$, in bits.

cards.q: What is the Nyquist theorem?
cards.a: To reconstruct a wave faithfully you must sample at more than **twice** its highest frequency. Human hearing reaches about $20\,\text{kHz}$, hence a $44.1\,\text{kHz}$ sample rate.

cards.q: What is aliasing?
cards.a: When sampling too slowly makes a high frequency indistinguishable from a lower one, so the reconstruction contains a tone that was never there.

cards.q: What is quantisation error?
cards.a: The difference between the true amplitude and the nearest value the bit depth can represent. It is heard as noise, and halves with each extra bit.

practice.q: An uncompressed image is $1920 \times 1080$ pixels with a colour depth of 24 bits. Calculate its file size in megabytes.
points: Approximately $6.22\,\text{MB}$, or $5.93\,\text{MiB}$.

practice.q: Explain the effect on file size and on image quality of doubling both the width and the height of an image in pixels.
points: The number of pixels increases by a factor of four, not two.
File size therefore quadruples, assuming colour depth is unchanged.
More detail can be captured, though quality only improves if the extra detail was present in the original.

practice.q: A 30-second stereo recording uses a sample rate of 44.1 kHz and a bit depth of 16. Calculate the uncompressed file size in megabytes.
points: $44{,}100 \times 16 = 705{,}600$ bits per second per channel.
Two channels gives $1{,}411{,}200$ bits per second.
Over 30 seconds that is $42{,}336{,}000$ bits.
$= 5{,}292{,}000$ bytes, approximately $5.29\,\text{MB}$.

practice.q: Explain, with reference to the Nyquist theorem, why audio is sampled at 44.1 kHz rather than 20 kHz.
points: Human hearing extends to roughly $20\,\text{kHz}$.
Nyquist requires a sample rate more than twice the highest frequency to be reproduced.
Sampling at $20\,\text{kHz}$ would only capture frequencies up to $10\,\text{kHz}$, losing much of the audible range.
$44.1\,\text{kHz}$ exceeds twice $20\,\text{kHz}$, leaving margin for the filters used before sampling.

practice.q: Explain what aliasing is and how it can be avoided.
points: Sampling below the Nyquist rate causes a high frequency to be indistinguishable from a lower one.
The reconstructed signal therefore contains a tone that was not in the original.
It is avoided by raising the sample rate, or by filtering out frequencies above half the sample rate before sampling.

practice.q: Explain the trade-off involved in choosing a bit depth for audio.
points: Each sample must be rounded to the nearest representable value, producing quantisation error.
A greater bit depth gives finer steps, so the error and the resulting noise are smaller.
Each additional bit doubles the number of levels and improves the signal-to-noise ratio by about 6 dB.
However file size grows in proportion to bit depth, so beyond the point where error is inaudible the extra data is wasted.

practice.q: A school is digitising an archive of audio tapes of spoken interviews. Recommend a sample rate and bit depth, justifying your choices.
points: Speech occupies a much narrower frequency range than music, roughly up to $8\,\text{kHz}$ for intelligibility.
A sample rate of around $16$–$22\,\text{kHz}$ therefore satisfies Nyquist for speech.
A bit depth of 16 gives ample dynamic range; 8 would introduce audible noise on quiet passages.
Mono is sufficient, since an interview has no meaningful stereo content, halving the size.
A clear recommendation is given and justified against the competing demand of archive storage cost.

pages.title: Compression
pages.lede: Making a file smaller by writing the same thing more cleverly, or by deciding some of it was not worth keeping.

cards.q: What is lossless compression?
cards.a: Compression from which the **original file can be reconstructed exactly**. Nothing is discarded, only re-described.

cards.q: What is lossy compression?
cards.a: Compression that discards information judged unimportant. The original cannot be recovered, but the files are far smaller.

cards.q: When must you use lossless compression?
cards.a: Whenever every byte matters — text, program code, spreadsheets, medical images, archives. A single changed bit can break a program or alter a diagnosis.

cards.q: Give two examples each of lossless and lossy formats.
cards.a: Lossless: PNG, FLAC, ZIP, GIF. Lossy: JPEG, MP3, MP4.

cards.q: What is run-length encoding?
cards.a: Replacing runs of the same value with the value and a count: `AAAAABBB` becomes `5A3B`. Very effective on flat areas, useless on noisy data.

cards.q: When does run-length encoding make a file bigger?
cards.a: When there are few runs. `ABCDE` becomes `1A1B1C1D1E`, twice the size — every symbol now carries a count of one.

cards.q: What is dictionary compression?
cards.a: Building a table of repeated sequences and replacing each occurrence with a short reference to the table. This is how ZIP and PNG work.

cards.q: How does Huffman coding save space?
cards.a: By giving **frequent symbols short codes and rare symbols long ones**, rather than the fixed width every symbol has in ASCII.

cards.q: What is a prefix code, and why does Huffman need one?
cards.a: A code where no codeword is the start of another. It means the decoder never needs separators or lookahead — as soon as a codeword is recognised, it must be the right one.

cards.q: How does JPEG discard information?
cards.a: It exploits the eye's poor sensitivity to fine colour detail and to high-frequency change, storing those less precisely than brightness and broad shapes.

cards.q: What is compression ratio?
cards.a: Original size divided by compressed size. A $10\,\text{MB}$ file reduced to $2\,\text{MB}$ has a ratio of $5{:}1$.

cards.q: Why can a compressed file not be usefully compressed again?
cards.a: Good compression removes the redundancy that compression exploits. The result looks close to random, and there is no pattern left to exploit.

practice.q: Distinguish between lossless and lossy compression, giving an appropriate use for each.
points: Lossless compression allows the original file to be reconstructed exactly.
Lossy compression permanently discards data judged to be less noticeable.
Lossless is required where exactness matters, such as text, program files or archives.
Lossy is appropriate where some quality loss is acceptable in exchange for much smaller files, such as streaming music or photographs.

practice.q: Apply run-length encoding to the sequence `WWWWWWBBWWWW` and state the compression achieved.
points: Encoded as `6W2B4W`.
Original is 12 characters, encoded is 6 characters.
A compression ratio of $2{:}1$, that is a 50% reduction.

practice.q: Explain why run-length encoding is unsuitable for a photograph but well suited to a scanned line drawing.
points: A photograph has continuously varying pixel values, so runs of identical values are very short or absent.
Encoding would add a count to nearly every pixel, potentially increasing the file size.
A line drawing has large uniform areas of white and black, producing long runs that encode very compactly.

practice.q: Explain how Huffman coding reduces file size, referring to symbol frequency.
points: Fixed-length encodings such as ASCII use the same number of bits for every character regardless of how often it occurs.
Huffman assigns shorter codes to more frequent symbols and longer codes to rarer ones.
The total number of bits is therefore reduced, since common symbols dominate the message.
The codes form a prefix code, so the result can still be decoded unambiguously without separators.

practice.q: A file of 2000 characters uses only four distinct characters, with frequencies 1000, 600, 300 and 100. Calculate the saving from using 2-bit fixed codes rather than 8-bit ASCII, and comment on whether Huffman could do better.
points: ASCII requires $2000 \times 8 = 16{,}000$ bits; fixed 2-bit codes require $2000 \times 2 = 4000$ bits.
A saving of $12{,}000$ bits, that is 75%.
Huffman would do better still, because the frequencies are uneven, so the commonest character could be given a 1-bit code.

practice.q: Explain why compressing an already-compressed file rarely reduces its size, and may increase it.
points: Compression works by removing redundancy such as repetition and predictable patterns.
An effectively compressed file has had that redundancy removed already.
Its contents therefore resemble random data, offering no pattern to exploit.
The second pass still adds its own headers and dictionary, so the file can grow slightly.

practice.q: A hospital stores X-ray images and also publishes photographs on its website. Recommend a compression approach for each, justifying your choices.
points: X-rays require lossless compression, since discarded detail could hide or create an apparent abnormality.
A lossless format such as PNG, or a medical format with lossless encoding, is therefore appropriate despite the larger files.
Website photographs can use lossy compression, since small quality losses are not noticeable at screen size.
JPEG gives a much smaller file, so pages load faster and less bandwidth is used.
The distinction is justified by consequence of error, which is severe in one case and negligible in the other.

pages.title: Logic gates
pages.lede: The seven switches everything else is built from, what each one physically does, and why two of them could do the whole job alone.

cards.q: What is a logic gate?
cards.a: A circuit with one or more binary inputs and one binary output, whose output is a fixed function of its inputs. It is built from transistors and holds no memory.

cards.q: What does an AND gate output?
cards.a: $1$ only when **every** input is $1$. Written $A \cdot B$ or $AB$.

cards.q: What does an OR gate output?
cards.a: $1$ when **at least one** input is $1$. Written $A + B$. This is inclusive or — $1+1=1$, not $0$.

cards.q: What does a NOT gate do?
cards.a: Inverts its single input. Written $\overline{A}$ or $A'$. Also called an inverter.

cards.q: What does a NAND gate output?
cards.a: The opposite of AND: $0$ only when every input is $1$. Written $\overline{A \cdot B}$.

cards.q: What does a NOR gate output?
cards.a: The opposite of OR: $1$ only when every input is $0$. Written $\overline{A + B}$.

cards.q: What does an XOR gate output?
cards.a: $1$ when the inputs **differ**. Written $A \oplus B$. This is exclusive or, so $1 \oplus 1 = 0$.

cards.q: What does an XNOR gate output?
cards.a: $1$ when the inputs are the **same**. It is an equality test, written $\overline{A \oplus B}$.

cards.q: What does the small circle on a gate symbol mean?
cards.a: Inversion. A bubble on the output turns AND into NAND; a bubble on an input inverts that input before the gate acts.

cards.q: What is a universal gate?
cards.a: One from which every other gate can be built. **NAND** and **NOR** are each universal on their own.

cards.q: How do you make a NOT gate from a NAND gate?
cards.a: Tie both inputs together. $\overline{A \cdot A} = \overline{A}$.

cards.q: Why are real chips built mostly from NAND gates?
cards.a: NAND is universal, and in CMOS it needs fewer transistors than AND — four rather than six, since AND is a NAND with an inverter bolted on.

practice.q: Complete a truth table for a two-input XOR gate and state one practical use of it.
points: Rows $00 \to 0$ and $01 \to 1$ correct.
Rows $10 \to 1$ and $11 \to 0$ correct.
Identifies that the output is 1 when the inputs differ.
A valid use is given, such as the sum bit of a half adder, a parity check, or detecting a change between two signals.

practice.q: Explain the difference between OR and XOR, using a truth table row to illustrate it.
points: OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1, including when both are.
XOR gives 1 only when exactly one input is 1.
They differ on the row $A=1, B=1$, where OR gives 1 and XOR gives 0.

practice.q: Show how a NOT gate can be constructed from a single NAND gate.
points: Both inputs of the NAND gate are connected to the same signal $A$.
The output is therefore $\overline{A \cdot A}$.
Since $A \cdot A = A$, the output is $\overline{A}$, which is NOT.

practice.q: Show how an AND gate can be constructed using only NAND gates.
points: A first NAND gate takes inputs $A$ and $B$, giving $\overline{A \cdot B}$.
A second NAND gate has both inputs tied to that output, acting as an inverter.
The result is $\overline{\overline{A \cdot B}}$.
Double negation gives $A \cdot B$, which is AND. Two NAND gates are required.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by a universal gate and state which gates are universal.
points: A universal gate is one from which any other logic gate, and therefore any logic circuit, can be built.
NAND is universal.
NOR is also universal.

practice.q: Explain why manufacturers prefer to build circuits from NAND gates rather than from a mixture of AND, OR and NOT.
points: Only one type of gate needs to be designed, tested and fabricated, simplifying manufacture.
NAND is universal, so no functionality is lost.
In CMOS, NAND requires fewer transistors than AND, which is a NAND followed by an inverter.
Fewer transistors means smaller area, lower cost and lower power consumption.

practice.q: A security system sounds an alarm when the system is armed AND either the door sensor OR the window sensor is triggered. Write the Boolean expression and state the gates required.
points: Defines variables, for example $S$ armed, $D$ door, $W$ window.
Expression $S \cdot (D + W)$.
An OR gate combines $D$ and $W$.
An AND gate combines that result with $S$.

pages.title: Truth tables and Boolean algebra
pages.lede: Writing down everything a circuit does, then finding a smaller circuit that does exactly the same thing.

cards.q: How many rows does a truth table with $n$ inputs have?
cards.a: $2^n$. Three inputs give eight rows, four give sixteen. Each extra input doubles the work.

cards.q: How should the input columns of a truth table be ordered?
cards.a: Counting in binary from $000\ldots$ upwards. It guarantees every combination appears exactly once and makes the table easy to check.

cards.q: What is a minterm?
cards.a: A row of the truth table where the output is $1$, written as a product of every variable, each inverted if it is $0$ in that row.

cards.q: What is sum-of-products form?
cards.a: An OR of the minterms — one AND term per row where the output is $1$. Every truth table can be written this way directly.

cards.q: State the identity laws.
cards.a: $A \cdot 1 = A$ and $A + 0 = A$.

cards.q: State the null laws.
cards.a: $A \cdot 0 = 0$ and $A + 1 = 1$. An AND with zero, or an OR with one, ignores the other input entirely.

cards.q: State the complement laws.
cards.a: $A \cdot \overline{A} = 0$ and $A + \overline{A} = 1$. Something cannot be both true and false, and must be one of them.

cards.q: State the idempotent laws.
cards.a: $A \cdot A = A$ and $A + A = A$. Repeating an input changes nothing.

cards.q: State the absorption laws.
cards.a: $A + A \cdot B = A$ and $A \cdot (A + B) = A$. The second term adds no information the first does not already carry.

cards.q: State De Morgan's laws.
cards.a: $\overline{A \cdot B} = \overline{A} + \overline{B}$ and $\overline{A + B} = \overline{A} \cdot \overline{B}$. Break the bar, change the sign.

cards.q: What is the distributive law in Boolean algebra?
cards.a: $A \cdot (B + C) = A\cdot B + A \cdot C$, and unusually also $A + B \cdot C = (A+B)(A+C)$, which has no arithmetic counterpart.

cards.q: Why simplify a Boolean expression at all?
cards.a: Fewer gates means lower cost, less power, less heat, less board space, and a shorter path so the circuit settles sooner.

practice.q: Construct a truth table for $F = A \cdot \overline{B} + C$.
points: Table has three inputs and therefore eight rows, listed in binary order.
Intermediate column for $A \cdot \overline{B}$ is correct.
Output is 1 for rows where $C = 1$.
Output is also 1 for $A=1, B=0, C=0$, giving outputs $0,1,0,1,1,1,0,1$.

practice.q: Use De Morgan's laws to simplify $\overline{\overline{A} + \overline{B}}$.
points: Applies De Morgan to give $\overline{\overline{A}} \cdot \overline{\overline{B}}$.
Removes the double negations.
Final answer $A \cdot B$.

practice.q: Simplify $A \cdot B + A \cdot \overline{B}$, naming the laws used.
points: Factorises to $A \cdot (B + \overline{B})$ by the distributive law.
$B + \overline{B} = 1$ by the complement law.
$A \cdot 1 = A$ by the identity law.
Final answer $A$.

practice.q: Simplify $\overline{A}\cdot B + A \cdot B + A \cdot \overline{B}$.
points: Groups the first two terms as $B(\overline{A} + A)$.
Simplifies to $B$ using complement and identity laws.
Expression becomes $B + A\overline{B}$.
Final answer $A + B$, since $B + A\overline{B} = B + A$.

practice.q: Write the sum-of-products expression for a function that is 1 for the input combinations $A\overline{B}C$, $AB\overline{C}$ and $ABC$ only.
points: One product term written per specified combination.
Terms correctly formed with complements where a variable is 0.
Expression $A\overline{B}C + AB\overline{C} + ABC$, joined by OR.

practice.q: Explain why simplifying a Boolean expression before building the circuit is worthwhile, giving three distinct reasons.
points: Fewer gates are needed, so the circuit costs less to manufacture.
Fewer gates consume less power and generate less heat.
Less physical space is needed on the chip or board.
A shorter path from input to output means fewer gate delays, so the circuit settles faster.

practice.q: A circuit implements $F = (A + B) \cdot (A + C)$. Show that this equals $A + B \cdot C$ and comment on which implementation is preferable.
points: Expands the brackets to $A\cdot A + A \cdot C + B \cdot A + B \cdot C$.
Uses $A \cdot A = A$ to give $A + AC + AB + BC$.
Applies absorption, since $A + AC + AB = A$.
Result is $A + B\cdot C$, confirming the identity.
The simplified form uses two gates rather than three, so it is cheaper and has a shorter delay.

pages.title: Karnaugh maps
pages.lede: A way of simplifying Boolean expressions by looking rather than by algebra, and the reason its rows are numbered so strangely.

cards.q: What is a Karnaugh map?
cards.a: A truth table redrawn as a grid, arranged so that adjacent cells differ in exactly one variable. Groups of adjacent $1$s can then be read off as simplified terms.

cards.q: Why are the headings ordered $00, 01, 11, 10$ rather than $00, 01, 10, 11$?
cards.a: So that neighbouring cells differ in only one bit. That is **Gray code**, and it is what makes adjacency mean "one variable can be eliminated".

cards.q: What sizes may a group be?
cards.a: A power of two — $1, 2, 4, 8, 16$ — and rectangular. A group of three or six is not allowed.

cards.q: What does doubling the size of a group do to the term?
cards.a: It removes one more variable. A group of $2^k$ cells eliminates $k$ variables from the term.

cards.q: May groups overlap?
cards.a: Yes, and they often should. Overlapping costs nothing and usually allows larger, therefore simpler, groups.

cards.q: Does the map wrap around?
cards.a: Yes. Left and right edges are adjacent, as are top and bottom, because the Gray code ordering is cyclic. The four corners of a $4\times4$ map form a valid group.

cards.q: How do you read a group as a term?
cards.a: Keep only the variables that stay constant across the whole group. A variable that is $1$ throughout appears plain; one that is $0$ throughout appears inverted.

cards.q: What is a don't-care condition?
cards.a: An input combination that cannot occur, or whose output does not matter. It is marked $\times$ and may be treated as $0$ or $1$, whichever makes groups bigger.

cards.q: What is a prime implicant?
cards.a: A group that cannot be made any larger. The simplification is built from these.

cards.q: What is an essential prime implicant?
cards.a: A prime implicant covering at least one $1$ that no other prime implicant covers. It must appear in the final answer.

cards.q: Why do Karnaugh maps stop being used above about five variables?
cards.a: The grid becomes impossible to read, since adjacency can no longer be shown in two dimensions. Software uses the Quine–McCluskey algorithm instead.

practice.q: Explain why the column headings of a Karnaugh map are written in the order $00, 01, 11, 10$.
points: The ordering ensures adjacent columns differ in exactly one variable.
This is Gray code ordering rather than ordinary binary counting.
It means that two adjacent cells can be combined to eliminate the variable that changes between them.

practice.q: A function of variables $A$ and $B$ gives output 1 for $\overline{A}B$, $A\overline{B}$ and $AB$. Use a Karnaugh map to simplify it.
points: Map drawn correctly with 1s in three of the four cells.
A group of two covering $A\overline{B}$ and $AB$ gives $A$.
A group of two covering $\overline{A}B$ and $AB$ gives $B$, with the overlap permitted.
Simplified expression $A + B$.

practice.q: State the rules governing the formation of groups on a Karnaugh map.
points: Groups must contain only 1s (or 1s and don't-cares).
The number of cells in a group must be a power of two.
Groups must be rectangular and may wrap around the edges of the map.
Groups should be as large as possible and may overlap; every 1 must be in at least one group.

practice.q: Explain what a don't-care condition is and why including one can improve a simplification.
points: It is an input combination that cannot occur, or whose output is irrelevant to the system.
It may be treated as either 0 or 1 without affecting correctness.
Treating it as 1 can allow a larger group to be formed.
A larger group eliminates more variables, giving a simpler expression and fewer gates.

practice.q: A three-input function outputs 1 for minterms 0, 1, 2, 5 and 6. Simplify it using a Karnaugh map.
points: Map drawn with the correct five cells set to 1.
Group covering minterms 0 and 1 gives $\overline{A}\,\overline{B}$.
Group covering minterms 2 and 6 gives $B\overline{C}$.
Group covering minterms 1 and 5 gives $\overline{B}C$.
A correct simplified expression such as $\overline{A}\,\overline{B} + B\overline{C} + \overline{B}C$ is stated.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a prime implicant and an essential prime implicant.
points: A prime implicant is a group that cannot be enlarged further.
An essential prime implicant covers at least one 1 that no other prime implicant covers.
Essential prime implicants must be included in the final expression, while other prime implicants may sometimes be omitted.

practice.q: Compare simplification by Boolean algebra with simplification by Karnaugh map.
points: Algebra requires choosing which law to apply, so it depends on insight and can miss simplifications.
A Karnaugh map is systematic, and a correctly grouped map is guaranteed to give a minimal sum of products.
Maps are limited to about four or five variables before adjacency cannot be shown on a grid.
Algebra has no such limit, and is the only option for larger functions done by hand.

pages.title: Building real circuits
pages.lede: Adders, multiplexers, decoders and the first circuit that can remember something — plus what happens in the nanoseconds before a circuit settles.

cards.q: What does a half adder do?
cards.a: Adds two single bits, producing a **sum** and a **carry**. Sum is $A \oplus B$; carry is $A \cdot B$.

cards.q: Why is a half adder not enough to add multi-bit numbers?
cards.a: It has no carry **in**, so it cannot accept the carry produced by the column to its right.

cards.q: What does a full adder do?
cards.a: Adds three bits — $A$, $B$ and a carry in — producing a sum and a carry out. Chaining them adds numbers of any width.

cards.q: Give the expressions for a full adder.
cards.a: $S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in}$ and $C_{out} = A\cdot B + C_{in}\cdot(A \oplus B)$.

cards.q: What is a ripple-carry adder, and what limits it?
cards.a: Full adders chained so each carry feeds the next. It is limited by delay: the top bit cannot settle until the carry has rippled through every stage.

cards.q: What does a multiplexer do?
cards.a: Selects one of several inputs and passes it to the single output, according to a select signal. A $2{:}1$ mux is $F = \overline{S}\cdot A + S \cdot B$.

cards.q: What does a decoder do?
cards.a: Takes an $n$-bit input and raises exactly one of its $2^n$ outputs — the one whose number matches the input. It is how an address selects a memory location.

cards.q: What is a combinational circuit?
cards.a: One whose output depends only on its current inputs. It has no memory.

cards.q: What is a sequential circuit?
cards.a: One whose output depends on its inputs **and** its previous state. It contains feedback, and therefore memory.

cards.q: How does an SR latch store a bit?
cards.a: Two NOR (or NAND) gates cross-coupled, so each drives the other's input. The pair has two stable states and stays in whichever it was last put into.

cards.q: What is propagation delay?
cards.a: The time a gate takes to change its output after its input changes. It is why a circuit's answer is not instantaneous.

cards.q: What is a hazard or glitch?
cards.a: A brief incorrect output produced while a circuit settles, caused by two paths to the same gate having different delays.

practice.q: Draw a truth table for a half adder and state the Boolean expressions for both outputs.
points: Table has four rows for inputs $A$ and $B$.
Sum column reads $0, 1, 1, 0$.
Carry column reads $0, 0, 0, 1$.
Expressions given as $S = A \oplus B$ and $C = A \cdot B$.

practice.q: Explain why a full adder is needed to add binary numbers of more than one bit.
points: Adding a column may produce a carry that must be added into the next column.
A half adder has no input for an incoming carry, so it cannot accept it.
A full adder takes three inputs, allowing carries to be chained from one column to the next.

practice.q: A 32-bit ripple-carry adder is built from full adders each with a propagation delay of 2 ns. Calculate the worst-case time for the result to settle, and explain the cause.
points: The carry must pass through all 32 stages in the worst case.
$32 \times 2 = 64\,\text{ns}$.
Each stage cannot compute its carry out until it has received its carry in.
The delay is therefore proportional to the number of bits, which is why faster carry schemes are used in practice.

practice.q: Describe the function of a multiplexer and give one use for it.
points: It selects one of several data inputs according to the value of a select input.
The selected input is passed to the single output.
A valid use is given, such as sharing one bus between several sources, or choosing which register feeds the ALU.

practice.q: Distinguish between combinational and sequential circuits, giving an example of each.
points: A combinational circuit's output depends only on its current inputs.
An example is an adder, a multiplexer or a decoder.
A sequential circuit's output depends on previous inputs as well, so it has memory.
An example is a latch, a flip-flop or a counter, and it contains feedback.

practice.q: Explain how an SR latch is able to store a bit.
points: Two gates are cross-coupled so that each one's output feeds the other's input.
This feedback means the circuit has two stable states.
Setting S drives the output to 1 and the feedback holds it there once S returns to 0.
Setting R drives it to 0 and the feedback holds that, so the last input is remembered.

practice.q: Explain what causes a glitch in a combinational circuit and discuss whether it matters.
points: Different paths from an input to the same gate may pass through different numbers of gates.
Signals therefore arrive at different times, and the gate briefly sees an inconsistent combination.
The output shows a short incorrect pulse before settling to the correct value.
In a synchronous design it usually does not matter, because the output is only sampled at the clock edge, after settling.
It does matter if the output feeds an asynchronous input such as a latch enable, where a transient pulse could be stored.

pages.title: What an operating system does
pages.lede: The program whose job is to stop every other program from having to know how the machine works — and from wrecking each other.

cards.q: What is an operating system?
cards.a: The software that manages the hardware and provides services to every other program. Nothing else has to know what disc or graphics card is fitted.

cards.q: Name the main functions of an operating system.
cards.a: Process and processor management, memory management, file management, device and input/output management, security and user accounts, and providing a user interface.

cards.q: What is a process?
cards.a: A program **in execution**, together with everything it needs to run: its memory, its registers, its open files and its current position in the code.

cards.q: What is multitasking?
cards.a: Running several processes on one processor by switching between them so quickly that all appear to progress at once.

cards.q: What is a context switch?
cards.a: Saving one process's registers and state, then loading another's, so execution can resume exactly where it left off. It is pure overhead — no useful work happens during it.

cards.q: What is a device driver?
cards.a: Software that translates the operating system's general requests into the specific commands a particular piece of hardware understands.

cards.q: Why is a driver needed at all?
cards.a: Every device is different. Without drivers, every application would need code for every model of printer, disc and graphics card in existence.

cards.q: What is the kernel?
cards.a: The core of the operating system, always in memory, running with full hardware privileges and handling the most fundamental services.

cards.q: What is the difference between kernel mode and user mode?
cards.a: Kernel mode allows any instruction and access to all memory. User mode forbids privileged instructions, so an ordinary program cannot touch hardware or other processes directly.

cards.q: What is a system call?
cards.a: A controlled request from a user-mode program asking the kernel to do something privileged on its behalf, such as reading a file.

cards.q: What does the file system do?
cards.a: Presents storage as named files in a hierarchy of folders, while tracking where the blocks actually are on the physical medium.

practice.q: Describe four functions of an operating system.
points: Process management — creating, scheduling and terminating processes.
Memory management — allocating memory to processes and preventing them accessing each other's.
File management — organising storage into named files and directories and controlling access.
Device management, security, or providing a user interface, correctly described.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a program and a process.
points: A program is a passive file of instructions stored on disc.
A process is that program actually running, with memory allocated and a current execution position.
One program may have several processes running from it at once, each with its own state.

practice.q: Explain what happens during a context switch and why it represents overhead.
points: The current process's registers, program counter and state are saved.
The next process's saved state is loaded into the registers.
Execution resumes in the new process exactly where it previously stopped.
No useful work is done during the switch, so time spent switching is time not spent computing.

practice.q: Explain why operating systems distinguish between kernel mode and user mode.
points: Kernel mode permits privileged instructions and unrestricted access to memory and hardware.
User mode blocks those instructions, so an application cannot access hardware directly.
A faulty or malicious program is therefore unable to damage other processes or the system itself.
Programs must instead make system calls, which the kernel can check before acting.

practice.q: Explain the purpose of a device driver.
points: It translates general operating system requests into the specific commands a particular device understands.
It hides the differences between devices of the same type behind a common interface.
Applications and the operating system therefore need no knowledge of the specific hardware fitted.

practice.q: A user reports that their computer has become unresponsive while a single application is running. Explain how the operating system is expected to prevent one program monopolising the machine.
points: The scheduler allocates each process a limited slice of processor time.
A timer interrupt returns control to the operating system when the slice expires.
The scheduler can then pre-empt the running process and give the processor to another.
Without pre-emption, a process that never yields would run indefinitely, which is what the symptom suggests.

practice.q: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of an operating system providing a layer of abstraction over the hardware.
points: Applications are written once against a common interface rather than for each device.
Hardware can be replaced or upgraded without rewriting applications.
The abstraction allows access control, so processes cannot interfere with one another.
However each layer adds overhead, so operations are slower than direct hardware access.
Some specialised software, such as real-time or high-performance systems, may need to bypass it, and a reasoned judgement is offered.

pages.title: Scheduling and interrupts
pages.lede: Deciding which process runs next, why every fair answer is unfair to somebody, and how the machine gets interrupted mid-sentence.

cards.q: What is scheduling?
cards.a: Deciding which of the ready processes gets the processor next, and for how long.

cards.q: What is first come first served?
cards.a: Processes run to completion in arrival order. Simple, but one long job delays everything behind it.

cards.q: What is the convoy effect?
cards.a: Under first come first served, a single long process holds up many short ones behind it, ruining the average waiting time.

cards.q: What is shortest job first?
cards.a: The process with the smallest expected run time goes next. Best average waiting time, but it needs run times known in advance and can starve long jobs.

cards.q: What is round robin?
cards.a: Each process gets a fixed time slice in turn; if it does not finish it goes to the back of the queue. Nobody starves and response time is predictable.

cards.q: What is a time slice or quantum?
cards.a: The longest a process may run before being pre-empted. Too long and the system feels unresponsive; too short and context switching wastes the processor.

cards.q: What is pre-emption?
cards.a: Taking the processor away from a running process before it has finished, so the operating system stays in control.

cards.q: What is starvation?
cards.a: When a process never gets the processor because higher-priority work keeps arriving. Priority schedulers are vulnerable to it.

cards.q: What is ageing?
cards.a: Gradually raising the priority of a process that has waited a long time, so it eventually runs. It is the standard cure for starvation.

cards.q: What is an interrupt?
cards.a: A signal that causes the processor to suspend what it is doing and run a handler. It is how hardware gets attention without being asked.

cards.q: What happens when an interrupt occurs?
cards.a: The current instruction finishes, the processor's state is pushed onto a stack, the handler's address is loaded into the PC, the handler runs, and the saved state is restored.

cards.q: What is polling, and why are interrupts usually better?
cards.a: Polling means repeatedly asking a device whether it is ready, which wastes processor time. An interrupt lets the device speak up only when something has happened.

practice.q: Three processes arrive at time 0 with burst times of 12 ms, 3 ms and 5 ms. Calculate the average waiting time under first come first served in that order, and under shortest job first.
points: FCFS waiting times are $0$, $12$ and $15$ ms.
FCFS average is $(0+12+15)/3 = 9$ ms.
SJF order is 3, 5, 12 with waiting times $0$, $3$ and $8$ ms.
SJF average is $(0+3+8)/3 \approx 3.67$ ms, which is lower.

practice.q: Explain the convoy effect and state which scheduling algorithm suffers from it.
points: A long-running process occupies the processor while short processes wait behind it.
Average waiting time rises sharply even though the total work is unchanged.
It affects first come first served, which is non-pre-emptive and runs in arrival order.

practice.q: Explain the effect of choosing a very short time quantum, and of choosing a very long one, in round robin scheduling.
points: A very short quantum means processes are switched frequently.
A large proportion of processor time is then spent context switching rather than doing useful work.
A very long quantum means a process may run for a long time before being pre-empted.
Interactive processes then wait longer, so the system feels unresponsive, and behaviour approaches first come first served.

practice.q: Explain what starvation is and describe one technique for preventing it.
points: A low-priority process never runs because higher-priority processes keep arriving.
Ageing gradually increases the priority of processes that have been waiting.
Eventually the waiting process's priority is high enough for it to be scheduled.

practice.q: Describe the sequence of events that occurs when an interrupt is received.
points: The processor completes the instruction currently being executed.
The contents of the registers and program counter are saved, typically on a stack.
The address of the appropriate interrupt service routine is loaded into the program counter and the handler executes.
The saved state is restored and the interrupted program resumes where it left off.

practice.q: Compare interrupts with polling as ways of handling input from a keyboard.
points: Polling requires the processor to check the keyboard repeatedly whether or not a key has been pressed.
Most checks find nothing, so processor time is wasted.
With interrupts the keyboard signals only when a key is pressed, so no time is spent checking.
Interrupts add complexity and a small handling latency, but are far more efficient for infrequent events.

practice.q: A system runs a mixture of interactive editing and long background rendering. Recommend a scheduling approach and justify it.
points: Interactive processes need short response times to feel usable.
Background rendering needs throughput but can tolerate delay.
A pre-emptive priority scheme with a short quantum for interactive work suits both.
Ageing should be applied so the rendering is not starved by continuous interaction.
A clear recommendation is stated and justified against both requirements.

pages.title: Translators
pages.lede: Getting from something a person can read to something a processor can execute, and the two very different bargains available for doing it.

cards.q: Why is a translator needed at all?
cards.a: A processor executes only machine code — binary patterns. Anything written in a higher-level language must be turned into those patterns before it can run.

cards.q: What is machine code?
cards.a: The binary instructions a particular processor executes directly. It is specific to that processor family, so it is not portable.

cards.q: What is assembly language?
cards.a: A human-readable form of machine code, with a mnemonic such as `ADD` for each instruction. One line of assembly is usually one machine instruction.

cards.q: What does an assembler do?
cards.a: Translates assembly language into machine code, essentially one-to-one, resolving labels into addresses.

cards.q: What does a compiler do?
cards.a: Translates an entire high-level program into machine code **once, before running**, producing an executable file.

cards.q: What does an interpreter do?
cards.a: Translates and executes the program **statement by statement, each time it runs**. No executable file is produced.

cards.q: Give two advantages of a compiler.
cards.a: The compiled program runs faster, since translation is already done, and the source code need not be given to the user.

cards.q: Give two advantages of an interpreter.
cards.a: Execution starts immediately with no compile step, and errors are reported with the line that caused them, which makes debugging quicker.

cards.q: How do compilers and interpreters differ in reporting errors?
cards.a: A compiler reports all syntax errors before anything runs. An interpreter reports one error at a time, only when execution reaches that line.

cards.q: What are the stages of compilation?
cards.a: Lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, code generation, and optimisation.
